sampling_model.design: Before outcomes are observed, the designer chooses any outcome-independent probability law on \(\mathcal A_K^n\), including arbitrary dependence and support on allocation faces. The attaining design assigns units independently with \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/2\) on active arms and probability zero on inactive arms; for support two this is equal randomization between the two active labels.
sampling_model.overlap: The unrestricted game imposes no overlap restriction. The proved all-count lower bound covers every realized count vector, including allocations entirely or partly to inactive arms and every face with zero count for one or more active arms.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no superpopulation nuisance estimation. For support two the construction has one contrast-orthogonal coordinate and reproduces the scalar base case; for support at least three, the finite response-alphabet dual score and all contrast-orthogonal tube directions resolve the multidimensional nuisance geometry.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: The unrestricted binary two-arm minimax risk is \(n^{-1}-C_An^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3})\), attained by Bernoulli randomization and nonlinear shrinkage.
comparator_promise_table.matched_by: Theorem 1 and the support-two reduction proposition

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: For bounded two-arm potential outcomes, independent assignment remains minimax when measurable estimators are unrestricted.

Theorem 2.1 gives permutation symmetrization and complete-randomization content, Theorem 3.1 reduces the minimax problem over linear-estimator schemes to minimization of a quadratic expected form subject to linear constraints over assignment and estimator schemes, and Theorem 3.2 gives the two-arm complete-randomization, Neyman-allocation, and difference-in-means specialization.

For two-arm controlled experiments, complete randomization is minimax for effect-estimation precision under a permutation-symmetric conditional-mean class, and inference-constrained mixed strategies optimize precision subject to design-uniformity constraints.
Under unbiased estimation of bounded finite-population totals, pairwise-independent sampling attains a sharp minimax bound.
Second-order minimax optimality can be characterized through positive solutions of a problem-specific Schrodinger equation.
Design-based estimators and variance adjustments are developed for pairwise contrasts in multi-armed randomized trials.
Adaptive treatment assignments are optimized for final multi-arm Stein-like shrinkage estimators by evaluating heteroscedastic Gaussian shrinkage risk.

body.tldr: For every fixed \(K\ge2\) and every zero-sum, \(\ell^1\)-normalized binary treatment contrast, the unrestricted finite-population design-estimation game has risk \(R_n(c)=n^{-1}-C_A V_c(s_c/2)^{2/3}n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3})\). Contrast-weighted independent assignment and a total full-label nonlinear Airy estimator attain the coefficient. The published two-arm theorem is the support-two base case, including the same contrast embedded among inactive labels; the new response-alphabet tube closes support at least three and proves the lower bound uniformly over dependent outcome-independent designs and every zero-count face. For rational contrasts, a terminating proof-producing procedure returns a finite record and a total evaluator for exact all-future risk brackets; rational bracketing transfers the mathematical expansion, but not Turing evaluation, to an unrepresented real contrast.

project_justification.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026), Theorems 2.2 and 3.1, solve the unrestricted binary support-two game through a scalar ancillary experiment and an Airy least-favorable prior. Hull (2026), Theorem 1, independently reduces the bounded two-arm game. Neither source supplies the finite response-alphabet curvature, multidimensional nuisance tube, or design-uniform all-face lower bound needed when at least three contrast coefficients are active; neither states the support-two result embedded among arbitrary inactive labels as part of one all-contrast theorem.
project_justification.niche: The natural parameter class consists of every fixed zero-sum, \(\ell^1\)-normalized contrast. On support two, normalization forces coefficients \(+1\) and \(-1\), so the gauge is one and the published scalar law is the base case. On support at least three, the response-alphabet gauge isolates the cusp while a target direction plus \(\ker(c^\top)\) supplies exact-target nuisance directions, including directions invisible on every missing-active-arm face.
project_justification.fill: The paper proves the Airy expansion on this single natural class, identifies the coefficient \(C_AV_c(s_c/2)^{2/3}\), constructs the contrast-weighted independent design and total nonlinear estimator, and proves a matching finite-schedule Bayes lower bound uniformly over every dependent outcome-independent assignment law, inactive-arm allocation, and missing-active-arm face. It also gives a finite proof-checkable certificate record with a total exact per-sample-size evaluator for rational inputs and a continuity transfer for arbitrary real contrasts.

body.related_work: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026), Theorems 2.1--2.3 and 3.1 and Appendix C, provide the scalar support-two benchmark: a finite reduction, nonlinear Airy shrinkage, and discretized least-favorable priors. The present support-two reduction recovers that coefficient and shows that embedding the contrast among inactive labels does not change the expansion; the new content is the response-alphabet and all-face closure for support at least three. Hull (2026), Theorem 1 and its symmetrization proof, also remains two-arm. Bai (2023), Theorems 2.1--3.2, treats permutation symmetrization and linear-estimator design problems rather than arbitrary nonlinear estimators in the fixed binary-schedule game. Kallus (2021) studies a different minimax-variance objective over a conditional-mean class. Aronow and Lopatto (2026), Theorems 2 and 3, impose unbiasedness. Levit (1986) supplies the positive-eigenfunction architecture connecting second-order minimax risk to a Schrodinger ground state. Schochet (2018) develops conventional design-based multi-arm estimators but not the unrestricted second-order minimax law. Rosenman and Hunter (2026) optimize adaptive assignments for heteroscedastic Gaussian shrinkage risk, a different adaptive decision problem. Hammer et al. (1996) supplies the four-regimen application rather than a theorem comparator.
body.interpretation: The coefficient separates a universal one-dimensional Airy phenomenon from finite response-alphabet geometry. Support two has curvature one, even inside a larger arm list; with at least three active coefficients, \(V_c(s_c/2)\) measures the exact cost of representing the target direction by binary response types. The all-count certificate shows why correlation, inactive-arm allocation, and zero-count faces cannot beat the contrast-weighted product design at second order.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The expansion is pointwise for each fixed arm count and fixed contrast. Remainder constants may deteriorate as an active weight approaches zero, so the theorem does not claim growing-\(K\) or vanishing-weight uniformity. The exact evaluator accepts rationally represented contrasts; continuity gives a mathematical extension to arbitrary reals but no algorithm for an unrepresented real input.
body.honest_scope: The theorem covers one natural class: every fixed \(K\ge2\) zero-sum, \(\ell^1\)-normalized contrast over fixed binary potential-outcome schedules. The published \(K=2\) law is its support-two base case, and the generalized reduction also permits inactive labels when \(K>2\); the new theorem content is the support-at-least-three response-alphabet closure and uniform control of all allocation faces. Designs may be arbitrarily dependent but must be chosen without observing the schedule, and estimators may be randomized functions of all labels and observed outcomes. No growing-arm, vanishing-weight-uniform, weak-null-inference, covariate-balancing, or interval-valued endpoint claim is made. The effective theorem returns exact all-future brackets only for rational inputs, while rational approximation transfers the mathematical coefficient to real contrasts without claiming a Turing evaluator for an unrepresented real.
